bibl.title: The exploration of continuous learning intention in STEAM education through attitude, motivation, and cognitive load

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The results showed that perceived usability directly influenced learning intention and strengthened the relationship between learning attitudes and intention.

span.label: continuous learning intention in STEAM education
span.quote: Therefore, this study aims to explore the latent factors that can enhance STEAM continuous learning intention.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: The data collection period was from February to May 2021, and 145 questionnaire responses were collected, yielding 141 valid responses.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: successfully carrying out the hands-on STEAM activity in the psychomotor phase raises the learner's attitude and motivation, which in turn produces the intention to keep learning
span.quote: In the third phase (affective domain), the successful implementation experience of STEAM activity in the second phase would increase the positive attitude and enhance the motivation towards continuous learning intention in the fourth phase.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a heavy cognitive load depresses learning performance because a learner cannot process the complexity and volume of the incoming information all at once
span.quote: In the second phase (psychomotor domain), a heavy cognitive load may negatively affect learning performance because individuals cannot handle the complexity and the infinity of the abundant information at once as an input

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: high demand from cognitive processes such as recall, comprehension, application and analysis consumes capacity and thereby lowers the learner's perception of the material's usability
span.quote: The high-level load of cognitive processes (such as knowledge recall, comprehension of understanding, application, and analysis) decreases perception

span.label: The paper flags its own limitations explicitly before listing them.
span.note: what this limits: the paper's own framing: DESPITE THE CONTRIBUTIONS OF THIS STUDY, SEVERAL LIMITATIONS REMAIN TO BE ADDRESSED
span.quote: Despite the contributions of this study, several limitations remain to be addressed.

span.label: The sample comes from a single region of Taiwan.
span.note: what this limits: the population the result speaks for: A SAMPLE OF STUDENTS FROM ONLY ONE REGION OF TAIWAN
span.quote: First, due to time limitations and lack of sufficient course support, the present study included a sample of students from only one region of Taiwan.

span.label: Variables linking AI-based STEM education to employability were not modelled.
span.note: what this limits: any employability claim: THE LONG-STANDING UNSOLVED PROBLEM OF AI-BASED EDUCATION IN STEM STUDIES AND EMPLOYABILITY NEEDS TO BE CONSIDERED WITH OTHER POSSIBLE VARIABLES
span.quote: Third, the long-standing unsolved problem of AI-based education in STEM studies and employability needs to be considered with other possible variables to examine the hypotheses in future studies (Chu et al., 2019).

span.label: Generalisation across two very different populations is established by the ABSENCE of a significant difference, which is an acceptance of the null.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that this model holds for both elementary and university students: it rests on finding no significant difference between the two groups, not on a test of equivalence
span.quote: all hypotheses in our structural model have no significant difference between elementary student group and university group as shown in Table 7. Therefore, our research result can be interpreted as generalization for both elementary and university students.

span.label: Items were removed from the model until the validity thresholds were satisfied, so the thresholds were met partly by deletion.
span.note: what this limits: the reported validity statistics: items were extracted from the model, after which all values exceeded the minimum threshold
span.quote: these items were extracted from the model. Therefore, all values exceeded the minimum threshold, indicating that the constructs were explained

span.label: Participation was voluntary and recruitment happened in class after the activity, so the sample is self-selected among those who had just taken part.
span.note: what this limits: this sample as representative of STEAM learners: students were recruited in the classroom after their learning activities and participated voluntarily
span.quote: In this study, elementary and university students were recruited in the classroom after their learning activities. The participants voluntarily participated in the questionnaire survey.

span.label: cognitive load theory, originally developed from short-term memory experiments, is imported as the cognitive-domain measure in a STEAM education acceptance model
span.quote: Cognitive load theory was first proposed by a cognitive psychologist based on empirical research on short-term memory ability

span.label: cognitive load
span.quote: Technology usage in STEAM education also has the benefits of decreasing cognitive load (mental load and mental effort) and improving students’ learning intentions

span.label: mental effort
span.quote: Technology usage in STEAM education also has the benefits of decreasing cognitive load (mental load and mental effort)

span.label: discriminant validity
span.quote: Discriminant validity is measured by the square root of the AVE of each latent variable, which indicates that each construct’s correlation is higher than the other constructs’ correlations

span.label: cognitive load - operationalised here as TWO components, mental load and mental effort, inside a model that also carries technology-acceptance and motivation constructs
span.quote: Technology usage in STEAM education also has the benefits of decreasing cognitive load (mental load and mental effort) and improving students’ learning intentions

span.label: generalization - established by a NON-SIGNIFICANT group difference rather than by sampling both populations to a defined standard
span.quote: Therefore, our research result can be interpreted as generalization for both elementary and university students.

span.label: extends → Weng et al. (2018)
span.quote: The results show that cognitive load enables learners to easily understand and implement the STEAM task, which extends the findings of Weng et al.

span.label: replicates → Davis, 1989; Davis et al., 1989 (TAM)
span.quote: The research results confirmed the relationship in Davis’s TAM constructs (Davis, 1989; Davis et al., 1989) that were applied to explain the behavioral intention of STEAM education (Mutambara & Bayaga, 2021; Su, 2019).

span.label: mental effort —part-of→ cognitive load
span.quote: Technology usage in STEAM education also has the benefits of decreasing cognitive load (mental load and mental effort)

span.label: structural equation modelling (partial least squares)
span.quote: This study employed partial least squares (PLS) using SmartPLS software to estimate the parameters of the proposed model.

span.label: confirmatory factor analysis
span.quote: This study adopted confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to assess the measurement model in terms of convergent

span.label: Cronbach's alpha
span.quote: Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for each construct were as follows: perceived usability (0.96), perceived usefulness (0.95), perceived ease of use (0.91)

span.label: composite reliability and average variance extracted
span.term: composite reliability and average variance extracted
span.quote: The CR values of all constructs were greater than the suggested minimum of 0.7, all rho_A values were greater than 0.9, and all AVE values were greater than 0.5.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: results of HTMT inference at the 95% confidence level were obtained by conducting a bootstrapping procedure with a sample size of 5000.

span.label: variance inflation factor (multicollinearity check)
span.quote: This study used VIF to examine whether multicollinearity existed.

span.label: coefficient of determination
span.quote: The coefficient of determination (R2) measures the insample predictive power

span.label: effect size
span.quote: The f2 effect determines the change in the R2 value when a specified exogenous construct is omitted from the model in the range of 0.02, 0.15, and 0.35

span.label: multi-group comparison test
span.quote: The partial least squares multi-group analysis (PLS-MGA) method is a non-parametric significance test for the difference of group-specific results

span.label: goodness-of-fit residual index
span.quote: The SRMR value for the saturated model was 0.069, and the RMS_theta value was 0.16 close to 0, indicating a well-fitting model in this study.

span.label: Perceived usability had a direct positive effect on continuous learning intention and also strengthened the link between learning attitude and intention.
span.quote: The results showed that perceived usability directly influenced learning intention and strengthened the relationship between learning attitudes and intention.

span.label: Cognitive load had a significant negative direct effect on perceived usability (B = -0.32), so lower load meant higher perceived usability.
span.quote: Analysis of the effects of cognitive load (H4) (cognitive load → perceived usability) showed that the variable had significant negative direct effects on perceived usability (B = − 0.32, p < 0.01).

span.label: ARCS motivation had a positive and significant effect on learning attitude (B = 0.48).
span.quote: Regarding the effects of Keller’s ARCS theory, H5 (ARCS → learning attitude) showed a positive and significant effect (B = 0.48, p < 0.01).

span.label: Both moderation terms were significant: perceived usability moderated attitude to intention (B = 0.104) and ARCS moderated perceived usability to attitude (B = 0.082).
span.quote: the interaction term “perceived usability x attitude” is positive and significant for intention (B = 0.104, t-value = 3.13, p = 0.002), and the interaction term “ARCS x perceived usability” is positive and significant for attitude (B = 0.082, t-value = 2.03, p = 0.042).

span.label: The attitude-to-intention relationship was steeper for learners with high perceived usability than for those with low perceived usability.
span.quote: Perceived usability strengthens the positive relationship between attitude and intention.

span.label: All three core TAM paths were supported: perceived usability to attitude (0.41), attitude to intention (0.34), and perceived usability to intention (0.55).
span.quote: H1 (perceived usability → learning attitude) path showed a significant positive effect (B = 0.41, p < 0.005), H2 (learning attitude→ learning intention) path showed a strong significant effect (B = 0.34, p < 0.01)

span.label: None of the model's paths differed significantly between the elementary-school and university subsamples, so the model held for both age groups.
span.quote: The PLS-GMA result showed that all hypotheses in our structural model have no significant difference between elementary student group and university group

span.label: The structural model fitted the data well, with SRMR of 0.069 and RMS_theta of 0.16.
span.quote: The SRMR value for the saturated model was 0.069, and the RMS_theta value was 0.16 close to 0, indicating a well-fitting model in this study.

span.label: continuous learning intention
span.quote: Continuous learning intention refers to the learners’ willingness to engage or attend STEAM activity in the future.

span.label: perceived usability (second-order construct)
span.quote: study created a second-order construct, namely perceived usability, which includes three constructs (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived enjoyment) derived from TAM

span.label: cognitive load
span.quote: Cognitive load consists of two constructs: mental load and mental effort.

span.label: mental load versus mental effort
span.quote: Mental load represents the cognitive capacity required to process the complexity of a task, whereas mental effort reflects a learner’s cognitive capacity or resources that are allocated to complete the learning task

span.label: STEAM learning cycle
span.quote: This paper proposes a STEAM learning cycle that reveals four phases (cognitive, psychomotor, and affective domains, and continuous learning intention) for successful STEAM learning.

span.label: ARCS model
span.quote: The ARCS model includes four components: attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction (Keller, 1983).

span.label: cognitive load
span.quote: Hypothesis 4 (H4) Cognitive load has a negative and significant effect on perceived usability.

span.label: continuous learning intention
span.quote: Hypothesis 2 (H2) Attitude has a positive and significant effect on intention.

span.label: learning attitude
span.quote: In the mediation mechanism, learning attitudes acted as mediating variables.

span.label: ARCS motivation
span.quote: Hypothesis 7 (H7) ARCS positively moderates the relationship between perceived usability and attitude.

span.label: perceived usability
span.quote: Hypothesis 6 (H6) Perceived usability positively moderates the relationship between attitude and intention.

span.label: 145 — questionnaire responses collected, of which 141 were valid
span.quote: The data collection period was from February to May 2021, and 145 questionnaire responses were collected, yielding 141 valid responses.

span.label: 84 undergraduate students and 57 elementary students — composition of the voluntary survey sample
span.quote: Participation in the questionnaire survey was voluntary (84 undergraduate students and 57 elementary students), and the participants completed the questionnaire after STEAM teaching activities.

span.label: 7-point Likert scale — response format of the 52-item instrument (24 TAM, 8 cognitive load, 20 ARCS items)
span.quote: Thus, an instrument consisting of 24 items (TAM scale), 8 items (cognitive load scale), and 20 items (ARCS scale) rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”) was proposed in this study.

span.label: B = − 0.32, p < 0.01 — path coefficient from cognitive load to perceived usability
span.quote: Analysis of the effects of cognitive load (H4) (cognitive load → perceived usability) showed that the variable had significant negative direct effects on perceived usability (B = − 0.32, p < 0.01).

span.label: B = 0.48, p < 0.01 — path coefficient from ARCS motivation to learning attitude
span.quote: Regarding the effects of Keller’s ARCS theory, H5 (ARCS → learning attitude) showed a positive and significant effect (B = 0.48, p < 0.01).

span.label: B = 0.104, t-value = 3.13, p = 0.002 — interaction (moderation) effect of perceived usability on the attitude-intention path
span.quote: the interaction term “perceived usability x attitude” is positive and significant for intention (B = 0.104, t-value = 3.13, p = 0.002), and the interaction term “ARCS x perceived usability” is positive and significant for attitude (B = 0.082, t-value = 2.03, p = 0.042).

span.label: 0.069 — SRMR value for the saturated model, indicating acceptable fit
span.quote: The SRMR value for the saturated model was 0.069, and the RMS_theta value was 0.16 close to 0, indicating a well-fitting model in this study.

span.label: 0.96 — Cronbach's alpha for the perceived usability construct
span.quote: Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for each construct were as follows: perceived usability (0.96), perceived usefulness (0.95), perceived ease of use (0.91)
